n: Second Chronicles opens with Solomon securely established as king. The key to his success is stated first: the Lord was with him and made him great.

f.w: the LORD his God was with him

n: Solomon begins his reign by calling together the nation’s leaders — military officers, judges, governors, and family heads — to worship with him. He starts with God, not with politics.
They travel to Gibeon, a few miles northwest of Jerusalem, where Moses’ wilderness tabernacle still stood. The Chronicler explains why worship there was legitimate.

f.g: A town about six miles (10 km) northwest of Jerusalem.
A raised worship site; this one was approved because the tabernacle stood there.

n: At this time Israel’s worship was split in two: the ark was in a tent David had pitched in Jerusalem, while the tabernacle and altar remained at Gibeon. The temple would reunite them.
The bronze altar made by Bezaleel in Moses’ day stood at Gibeon. Solomon and the people came to seek the Lord there, linking his reign to Israel’s ancient worship.

f.g: The Spirit-filled craftsman who built the tabernacle furnishings.
Went there to seek the Lord, to inquire of Him in worship.

n: Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings — an extravagant act of devotion, showing his whole heart was turned toward God.
That night God appeared and offered Solomon anything he wished. It is a test of the heart: what would you ask for?

f.w: Ask what I shall give thee

n: Solomon begins with gratitude, recognizing that God showed great kindness to David and that his own kingship came from that mercy.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast, covenant love and loyal kindness.

n: He asks God to fulfill His promise to David. Solomon feels the weight of ruling a nation as numerous as the dust — echoing God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: like the dust of the earth

n: Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to lead and judge such a great people. “Go out and come in” means to lead in all of daily life, including war and public affairs.

f.g: Hebrew idiom for leading the people in all activities.

n: God is pleased that Solomon asked unselfishly — not for wealth, honor, revenge on enemies, or long life, but for wisdom to serve God’s people.

f.w: Because this was in thine heart

n: God grants wisdom and adds what Solomon didn’t ask for: unmatched riches and honor. When we seek first what God values, He often adds other blessings.
Solomon returns from Gibeon to Jerusalem to begin his reign in earnest.
Solomon builds a large chariot army and stations it in special chariot cities. Notably, Moses’ law had warned kings against multiplying horses.

f.g: Garrison towns built to house chariots and horses.

n: A picture of overflowing prosperity: silver and gold as common as rocks, and costly cedar as plentiful as the ordinary sycamore-fig trees of the foothills.

f.g: Sycamore-figs, common trees in Judah’s lowland, used for ordinary timber.
The Shephelah, the low hills west of Judah.

n: Solomon imported horses from Egypt and another source; his traders bought them at set prices. The Hebrew word translated “linen yarn” is now usually read as the place-name Kue (Cilicia).

f.g: Many scholars read Hebrew miqveh/qeve as ‘from Kue’ — Cilicia, in modern Turkey, a horse-trading region.

n: Solomon’s merchants acted as middlemen, selling chariots and horses to Hittite and Syrian kings. The details show how wealthy and far-reaching his trade had become.

f.g: A shekel weighed about 11.5 grams (0.4 oz).
Here, the neo-Hittite kingdoms of northern Syria.
